2016B16.goal: An infinite geometric series has positive sum $S$ and second term $1$. We want the least possible $S$. Express $S$ in terms of the ratio $r$ and minimise.

tools.name: Infinite geometric sum
tools.why: The partial sums converge to this when $|r|<1$.

2016B16.approach: The second term is $ar=1$, so $a=\tfrac1r$ and $S=\tfrac{1}{r(1-r)}$. For $S>0$ we need $0<r<1$. Minimising $S$ means maximising $r(1-r)$.

steps.title: Write $S$ in terms of $r$
steps.explain: $a=\tfrac1r$, so $S=\dfrac{1/r}{1-r}=\dfrac{1}{r(1-r)}$. If $-1<r<0$, then $r(1-r)<0$ and $S<0$, so $0<r<1$.

steps.title: Minimise
steps.explain: $r(1-r)\le\tfrac14$ with equality at $r=\tfrac12$. So $S\ge4$, achieved by $2+1+\tfrac12+\cdots$.

2016B16.recognize: Optimising a geometric series under a term condition: express the sum in $r$ and use a quadratic maximum.

2016B17.goal: Numbers $2$–$7$ go on the faces of a cube; each vertex gets the product of its three faces. We maximise the sum of the eight products. The sum factors neatly.

tools.name: Factoring the vertex sum
tools.why: With opposite faces $(a,b),(c,d),(e,f)$, each vertex picks one face from each pair; expanding the product gives all $8$ choices.

tools.name: Equal is best (AM-GM)
tools.fact: \text{fixed sum }\Rightarrow\text{product largest when factors are equal}
tools.why: $xyz\le\left(\tfrac{x+y+z}3\right)^3$.

2016B17.approach: Recognise the sum of products as $(a+b)(c+d)(e+f)$, a product of three pair sums totalling $27$. Make the three pair sums equal: $9,9,9$.

steps.title: Factor
steps.explain: Each vertex uses one face from each opposite pair. Expanding $(a+b)(c+d)(e+f)$ gives exactly the $8$ vertex products.

check.q: How many terms does $(a+b)(c+d)(e+f)$ have when expanded?

steps.title: Maximise
steps.explain: The three sums add to $2+\cdots+7=27$. The product is largest when they are equal, $9$ each: pairs $(2,7),(3,6),(4,5)$. Value $9^3=729$.

check.q: Which pairing gives three sums of $9$?

2016B17.bridge: Factor the sum and make the opposite-face sums equal.
solution: The sum of vertex products is $(a+b)(c+d)(e+f)$ for opposite pairs.
The three sums total $27$; the product is maximised when each is $9$.
2016B17.shortcut: "Sum over vertices of face products" always factors into opposite-pair sums.
traps: Putting the largest numbers together at one vertex.
2016B17.recognize: Sums of products over all choices factor as a product of sums; then maximise with equal factors.

2016B18.goal: We count ways to write $345$ as a sum of at least two consecutive positive integers. A run of $k$ terms starting at $a$ has sum $\tfrac{k(2a+k-1)}2$, so we need factorisations of $690$.

tools.name: Sum of consecutive integers
tools.why: Number of terms times the average.

tools.name: Opposite parity
tools.why: Their difference $2a-1$ is odd.

2016B18.approach: Set $k(2a+k-1)=690$ with $2\le k<2a+k-1$. Every factor pair $(k,m)$ with $k<m$ gives a valid run (parities automatically differ, since $690$ has exactly one factor $2$). Count pairs and drop $k=1$.

steps.title: Set up
steps.explain: $k(2a+k-1)=690$. Let $m=2a+k-1$; then $a=\tfrac{m-k+1}2$, a positive integer whenever $m>k$ and they have opposite parity.

steps.title: Count factor pairs
steps.explain: $690$ has $16$ divisors, giving $8$ pairs $k<m$. Since $690=2\times\text{odd}$, one factor of each pair is even and one odd. Exclude $k=1$: $7$ ways.

solution: A run of $k$ terms from $a$ sums to $\tfrac{k(2a+k-1)}2$, so $k(2a+k-1)=690$.
Each factor pair $k<m$ of $690$ gives one run (parities differ automatically).
2016B18.shortcut: The number of ways to write $n$ as a sum of consecutive positive integers (including the single term) equals the number of odd divisors of $n$: $345$ has $8$, minus $1$.
2016B18.recognize: Sums of consecutive integers: $k(2a+k-1)=2n$; count factor pairs with opposite parity (equivalently, odd divisors of $n$).

2016B19.goal: In a $5\times4$ rectangle, segments $AG$ and $AC$ cross $EF$ at $Q$ and $P$. We want $\tfrac{PQ}{EF}$. Parametrising $EF$ gives the positions of $P$ and $Q$ as fractions along it.

tools.name: Coordinates
tools.why: Read from $EB=1$, $CG=1$, $DF=2$.

tools.name: Parametrising $EF$
tools.why: $t$ is the fraction of the way from $E$ to $F$, so $PQ/EF=|t_P-t_Q|$.

2016B19.approach: Lines through $A$ are $y=mx$. Intersect each with the parametrised $EF$ to get $t$. The difference of the two $t$-values is the required ratio.

steps.title: Intersect $AG$
steps.explain: $AG$: $y=\tfrac35x$. $4t=\tfrac35(4-2t)$ gives $20t=12-6t$, $t_Q=\tfrac{6}{13}$.

steps.title: Intersect $AC$
steps.explain: $AC$: $y=\tfrac45x$. $4t=\tfrac45(4-2t)$ gives $5t=4-2t$, $t_P=\tfrac47$.

steps.title: Ratio
steps.explain: $\tfrac{PQ}{EF}=\tfrac47-\tfrac6{13}=\tfrac{52-42}{91}=\tfrac{10}{91}$.

2016B19.bridge: Parametrise $EF$ and intersect with both lines through $A$.
2016B19.shortcut: Because $t$ measures fraction along $EF$, you never need the length $EF$ itself.
traps: Computing actual distances and dividing (slower, error-prone).
Mixing up $P$ and $Q$ (sign does not matter for the ratio).
2016B19.recognize: Ratios of segments on a line cut by other lines: parametrise and compare parameter values.

2016B20.goal: A dilation sends the circle of radius $2$ at $A(2,2)$ to the circle of radius $3$ at $A'(5,6)$. We want how far the origin moves. A dilation has the form $P\mapsto kP+t$.

tools.name: Dilation formula
tools.why: A dilation scales all vectors by $k$ and then translates.

tools.name: Scale factor from radii
tools.why: Radius $2$ becomes radius $3$.

2016B20.approach: Find $k$ from the radii, then $t$ from $A\mapsto A'$. The origin goes to $t$, so the distance moved is $|t|$.

steps.title: Move the origin
steps.explain: $O'=k\cdot O+t=(2,3)$. Distance $\sqrt{4+9}=\sqrt{13}$.

check.q: What is the distance from $(0,0)$ to $(2,3)$?

2016B20.bridge: Write the dilation as $kP+t$, find $t$, and the origin moves to $t$.
2016B20.shortcut: The centre is $(-4,-6)$, but you never need it.
traps: Assuming the origin is the centre of dilation.
2016B20.recognize: Dilations and other similarity maps: write $P\mapsto kP+t$ and solve for unknowns from one known point.

2016B21.goal: We need the area enclosed by $x^2+y^2=|x|+|y|$. By symmetry, compute one quadrant and multiply by $4$.

tools.name: Symmetry
tools.fact: (x,y)\to(\pm x,\pm y)\text{ leaves the equation unchanged}
tools.why: Only $|x|$, $|y|$, $x^2$, $y^2$ appear.

tools.name: Completing the square
tools.why: Add $\tfrac14+\tfrac14$.

tools.name: Diameter recognition
tools.fact: (1,0)\text{ and }(0,1)\text{ are ends of a diameter}
tools.why: Their midpoint is the centre $(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$ and their distance is $\sqrt2=2r$.

2016B21.approach: In the first quadrant the curve is a circle through $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$. The enclosed piece there is the triangle with vertices $(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)$ plus the half-disc on the diameter from $(1,0)$ to $(0,1)$.

steps.title: First quadrant curve
steps.explain: $x^2+y^2=x+y$ is $(x-\tfrac12)^2+(y-\tfrac12)^2=\tfrac12$: centre $(\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$, radius $\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$. The points $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ are ends of a diameter.

steps.title: Area in one quadrant
steps.explain: The region is the right triangle $(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)$ (area $\tfrac12$) plus the outer half-disc on its hypotenuse (area $\tfrac12\pi\cdot\tfrac12=\tfrac\pi4$).

check.q: What is the area of a half-disc of radius $\tfrac1{\sqrt2}$?

steps.title: Total
steps.explain: $4\left(\tfrac12+\tfrac\pi4\right)=\pi+2$.

2016B21.bridge: Complete the square in one quadrant, split into triangle plus half-disc, and multiply by $4$.
solution: By symmetry, work in the first quadrant: $(x-\tfrac12)^2+(y-\tfrac12)^2=\tfrac12$.
The enclosed part there is the triangle $(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)$ plus the half-disc on diameter $(1,0)$–$(0,1)$: $\tfrac12+\tfrac\pi4$.
2016B21.shortcut: The full region is a square of side $\sqrt2$ (area $2$) with four half-discs (total area $\pi$) on its sides.
traps: Using the whole disc in each quadrant (it extends outside the quadrant).
2016B21.recognize: Equations with $|x|$ and $|y|$: use symmetry and work in one quadrant, completing the square.

2016B22.goal: In a round robin where every team went $10$–$10$, we count "cyclic" triples ($A$ beats $B$ beats $C$ beats $A$). Count the opposite: triples where one team beat both others.

tools.name: Number of teams
tools.why: Each team plays every other once.

tools.name: Non-cyclic triples
tools.why: In a triple, either there is a top team or the results form a cycle.

tools.name: Counting by the top team
tools.why: Choose two teams that the top team beat.

2016B22.approach: Total triples is $\binom{21}{3}$. A non-cyclic triple has a unique team that beat the other two; count such triples by choosing that team and two of its $10$ victims. Subtract.

steps.title: Total
steps.explain: $21$ teams, $\binom{21}{3}=1330$ triples.

steps.title: Non-cyclic
steps.explain: Each team is the top of $\binom{10}{2}=45$ triples: $21\cdot45=945$.

2016B22.bridge: Subtract the triples with a top team from all triples.
solution: Triples with a team beating both others: $21\binom{10}{2}=945$.
2016B22.shortcut: Cyclic triples $=\binom n3-\sum\binom{w_i}2$ for any tournament.
traps: Counting each non-cyclic triple more than once.
2016B22.recognize: Counting cyclic triangles in tournaments: subtract transitive triples, counted by their top vertex.

2016B23.goal: In a regular hexagon, lines $AB$, $ZW$, $YX$, $ED$ are parallel and equally spaced. Hexagon $WCXYFZ$ is the middle band of the big hexagon. We want its share of the area.

tools.name: Coordinates for a hexagon
tools.why: Side $1$, with $AB$ horizontal.

tools.name: Area by horizontal slices
tools.why: Between two horizontal lines, the band is a trapezoid when the side boundaries are straight.

tools.name: Hexagon area
tools.why: Six equilateral triangles.

2016B23.approach: The four lines are at heights $0,\tfrac{\sqrt3}3,\tfrac{2\sqrt3}3,\sqrt3$. Find the band's width at its bottom, middle ($C$ and $F$ level) and top, then add two trapezoids.

steps.title: Widths of the band
steps.explain: At height $\tfrac{\sqrt3}3$: $Z=(-\tfrac13,\tfrac{\sqrt3}3)$, $W=(\tfrac43,\tfrac{\sqrt3}3)$, width $\tfrac53$. At height $\tfrac{\sqrt3}2$ (through $F$ and $C$): width $2$. At height $\tfrac{2\sqrt3}3$: width $\tfrac53$ again.

check.q: How wide is a regular hexagon of side $1$ at the level of $C$ and $F$?

steps.title: Area of the band
steps.explain: Two trapezoids of height $\tfrac{\sqrt3}2-\tfrac{\sqrt3}3=\tfrac{\sqrt3}6$ with parallel sides $\tfrac53$ and $2$: $2\cdot\tfrac{11/3}{2}\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}6=\tfrac{11\sqrt3}{18}$.

steps.title: Ratio
steps.explain: Hexagon area $\tfrac{3\sqrt3}2$. Ratio $\tfrac{11\sqrt3/18}{3\sqrt3/2}=\tfrac{22}{54}=\tfrac{11}{27}$.

2016B23.bridge: Find the band's widths at three heights and add two trapezoids.
solution: With side $1$, the lines are at heights $0,\tfrac{\sqrt3}3,\tfrac{2\sqrt3}3,\sqrt3$.
The band $WCXYFZ$ has width $\tfrac53$ at its top and bottom and $2$ in the middle.
2016B23.shortcut: Each outer band is a trapezoid with parallel sides $1$ and $\tfrac53$ and height $\tfrac{\sqrt3}3$: $\tfrac{4\sqrt3}{9}$ each; subtract both from the hexagon.
traps: Assuming the three bands have equal area ($\tfrac13$).
Using the height between $AB$ and $ED$ as $2$.
2016B23.recognize: Regions cut from regular polygons by parallel lines: coordinates and horizontal widths turn areas into trapezoids.

2016B24.goal: We count four-digit $abcd$ whose two-digit pieces $\overline{ab}<\overline{bc}<\overline{cd}$ form an arithmetic sequence. The arithmetic condition is one linear equation in the digits.

tools.name: Arithmetic sequence
tools.why: The middle term is the average of its neighbours.

tools.name: Casework on one digit
tools.why: $b$ determines the size of the right side.

2016B24.approach: Turn the condition into $19b=10a+8c+d$. For each $b$, find digits $a\ge1$, $c$, $d$ satisfying it, and check that the sequence is increasing ($\overline{ab}<\overline{bc}$).

steps.title: Derive the equation
steps.explain: $2(10b+c)=10a+b+10c+d$ simplifies to $19b=10a+8c+d$.

2016B24.bridge: Reduce to $19b=10a+8c+d$ and do casework on $b$.
2016B24.shortcut: Many solutions are consecutive digits ($1234$, $2345$, …, $6789$) or "step $2$" patterns; casework catches the rest.
2016B24.recognize: Digit conditions involving overlapping two-digit numbers: expand into a single linear equation in digits and do casework.

2016B25.goal: $f(x)=\sum_{k=2}^{10}(\lfloor kx\rfloor-k\lfloor x\rfloor)$. We count distinct values for $x\ge0$. Each term depends only on the fractional part of $x$.

tools.name: Floor of a multiple
tools.why: Write $x=\lfloor x\rfloor+\{x\}$.

tools.name: Jump points
tools.why: It increases when $kt$ crosses an integer.

tools.name: Euler's totient
tools.why: Numerators coprime to $k$.

2016B25.approach: $f(x)=\sum_k\lfloor k\{x\}\rfloor$, a non-decreasing step function of $t=\{x\}\in[0,1)$. It jumps at every fraction $\tfrac jk$ with $2\le k\le10$. The number of values is $1$ plus the number of distinct jump points, which are the reduced fractions with denominators $2$ to $10$.

steps.title: Reduce to the fractional part
steps.explain: $\lfloor kx\rfloor-k\lfloor x\rfloor=\lfloor k\{x\}\rfloor$. So $f$ depends only on $t=\{x\}\in[0,1)$, and it is non-decreasing in $t$.

steps.title: Count jump points
steps.explain: $f$ jumps exactly at fractions in $(0,1)$ with denominator $\le10$. Distinct ones are reduced fractions $\tfrac jk$, counted by $\varphi(k)$: $\varphi(2..10)=1,2,2,4,2,6,4,6,4$, total $31$.

steps.title: Count values
steps.explain: Starting at $f=0$ for $t=0$, each of the $31$ jumps gives a new value: $32$ values.

check.q: If a step function starts at one value and jumps up $31$ times, how many values does it take?
check.why: Initial value plus one per jump.

2016B25.bridge: Reduce to $\{x\}$, count distinct jump fractions with $\varphi$, and add $1$.
solution: It jumps exactly at the reduced fractions $\tfrac jk\in(0,1)$ with $2\le k\le10$.
So $f$ takes $32$ values. The answer is $\textbf{(A)}\ 32$.
2016B25.shortcut: Count Farey fractions of order $10$ in $(0,1)$: $31$.
traps: Thinking $f$ grows without bound (it depends only on $\{x\}$).
2016B25.recognize: Sums like $\lfloor kx\rfloor-k\lfloor x\rfloor$: reduce to the fractional part; values change at fractions with small denominators.
